The Krait.
Kraits are known for biting people while they sleep,
so quietly that the sleeper may not even notice.
In two thousand and five, snakebites killed an estimated forty-five thousand nine hundred people in India,
and the common krait has long ranked among the four snakes most to blame.
In one Sri Lankan hospital study of common krait bites,
nine in ten happened at night.
Kraits also eat other snakes, including each other.
In western India, one common krait was recorded swallowing a smaller krait in about ten minutes.
So this is a night-time killer that eats its own relatives,
and surely nothing out there would hunt that.
Here's the twist: the king cobra does.
Not that exact krait, but its cousin:
researchers have reported king cobras eating banded kraits in the wild,
and the king cobra's genus name, Ophiophagus, literally means snake eater.
For the king cobra, kraits are simply a menu item.

The Scent Trail.
In southern India, researchers watched a radio-tagged king cobra
follow the scent of its prey twenty meters up into the trees.
It hunts with its tongue: it flicks the air,
picks up the smell another snake left behind, and follows it wherever it goes.
That same cobra tracked one trail back and forth across a fast stream three times,
and it kept following trails through heavy rain.
Once, the smell was so strong that it bit a stone.
Twice.
In India's Western Ghats, its usual target is the Indian rat snake.
It's harmless to people, it averages about one point seven five meters,
and it turns up around farms and rice fields, because farms have rats.
And the cobra covers serious ground to find one.
That tagged male moved more than thirty-five kilometers in under six months,
and in Thailand, tracked king cobras used areas averaging about five square kilometers each.
It's a bloodhound that only ever follows the scent of other dogs.

The Swallow.
A king cobra can swallow a rat snake more than half its own length,
without hands, without legs and without chewing.
In the Western Ghats, adult males usually measure three to four meters,
and king cobras can reach about five and a half,
the longest venomous snakes in the world.
Even so, swallowing something that long is a project.
Here's how it works: a snake's jaw is built from two independent bones
that are only loosely attached to the skull.

The Cobra.
A king cobra will eat a real cobra.

one of those four deadliest snakes from the start.
The awkward part is that the king cobra isn't technically a cobra at all.
True cobras belong to a group called Naja,
and king cobras have a genus all to themselves, Ophiophagus.
They are related, though, because both belong to the elapids,
the same venomous family as kraits and mambas.
It's a shark that hunts other sharks and, on paper, isn't even a shark.

The Pit Vipers.
One wild king cobra in southern India ate twenty-six venomous pit vipers in about four and a half months,
and researchers watched almost every meal.
He was a male a little over three meters long,
and he spent about half of his active hours hunting,
with a team following him every day from morning until nightfall.
Most of the vipers he caught were up in trees, shrubs or vines,
and he usually grabbed them right behind the head.
Here's the catch: pit vipers bite back,
and in nine of those hunts, the cobra appeared to get bitten.
Each time, he let go and waited, about ten minutes on average,
for his own venom to finish the job, and then he went back and ate.

The Monitor Lizard.
For an animal whose name means snake eater,
the king cobra has a real lizard habit.
In Thailand, researchers tracking king cobras by radio caught them eating clouded monitor lizards,
and they published it under a title calling the king cobra a supposed snake specialist.
In Singapore, one was seen swallowing a clouded monitor at night,
which is odd, because king cobras mostly hunt by day.
And in two thousand and twenty-two, on the Andaman Islands,
one was photographed eating a bullfrog,
the first time anyone had recorded a king cobra eating a frog.
Researchers in India had already noted that monitor lizards were the only prey besides snakes

The Nest.
The king cobra is the only snake known to build a nest for its eggs.
The female sweeps dead leaves together with her body
and carries them in tight coils, for days on end.
Then she crawls over the pile again and again to pack it down,
and burrows inside to hollow out a chamber.
A finished nest can be about fifty-five centimeters high and almost one and a half meters wide.
Inside go between fifteen and fifty eggs,
for seventy-five to a hundred days,
and she often stays on top of the nest the whole time.
It's like a parent building the nursery by hand, then sleeping on the roof of it for three months.
Here's the dark part:
keepers at the Bronx Zoo describe her instincts pushing her away from the eggs as they hatch.
Their explanation is that it stops her mistaking her own babies for food.
